blocks.prompt: Saturn and Its Rings
blocks.text: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun. It is a long way from us. Sunlight takes more than an hour to get there. Saturn is a ball of gas. There is no ground on Saturn. If you went there, you would have nothing to stand on. The best part is the rings. Saturn has thousands of rings around its middle. They are made of ice and dust. Some pieces are as small as a crumb. Some are as big as a car. They all race around Saturn together. The rings are very wide. They are also very thin, like a sheet of paper.

blocks.prompt: The Planet You Could Float in a Bathtub
blocks.text: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, and the second biggest in our solar system. You could line up more than nine Earths across its face. But size is not the strangest thing about it. Saturn is light. It is made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium, two of the lightest gases there are. Scientists have worked out that Saturn is less dense than water. If you could find a bathtub big enough, Saturn would float in it. Then there are the rings. From far away they look like smooth hoops of light. They are not solid at all. The rings are made of billions of chunks of ice, from grains of dust to boulders bigger than a bus. Each chunk is its own tiny moon, going around Saturn on its own path. The rings stretch about 170,000 miles across, but in most places they are only about ten yards thick. Imagine a sheet of paper the size of a city. That is the shape of Saturn's rings.

4.title: The Planet That Would Float
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium

Rings about 170,000 miles wide, about 10 yards thick
A six-sided storm sits over the north pole
The Cassini spacecraft studied it from 2004 to 2017
The rings may be younger than the dinosaurs

blocks.prompt: A World Without a Floor
blocks.text: Saturn is a world without a floor. It is the second largest planet in the solar system, wide enough to swallow more than seven hundred Earths, and yet it is made of almost nothing solid. Hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements in the universe, make up nearly all of it. Squeeze down through its yellow cloud tops and the gas around you thickens, and thickens, until it behaves like a liquid. There is no line where sky ends and ground begins. There is no ground. Because Saturn is so light for its size, it is less dense than water. Drop it into an ocean large enough and it would bob on the surface like a cork. The rings look solid from Earth, but they are not one object. They are billions of separate pieces of water ice, ranging from specks of dust to lumps the size of a house. Each piece orbits Saturn by itself. Together they form a disk about 170,000 miles wide and, in most places, only about ten yards thick. Scaled down to the width of a football field, the rings would be far thinner than a sheet of paper. Nobody is certain how old they are. For a long time people assumed the rings formed with the planet, four and a half billion years ago. Measurements from the Cassini spacecraft suggest something stranger. The rings may be only a hundred million years old or less, which means dinosaurs walked on Earth beneath a ringless Saturn. Cassini also found that the rings are slowly raining down into the planet. They are not permanent. We may simply have arrived at the right moment to see them.

notes: Galileo saw the rings in 1610 and thought they were handles

blocks.prompt: The Ornament We Arrived in Time to See
blocks.text: Galileo Galilei turned his telescope toward Saturn in 1610 and could not make sense of what he saw. The planet appeared to have handles, or ears, or perhaps two smaller companions pressed against its sides. He drew them carefully. Two years later he looked again and they were gone. Saturn had, in his words, swallowed its own children. Galileo never learned that he had been staring at a ring system tilted edge-on to his line of sight, thin enough to vanish. It took another forty-five years and a better telescope before Christiaan Huygens worked out the truth: Saturn is circled by a flat, solid-looking disk that touches the planet nowhere. Huygens was almost right. The disk is not solid. Saturn's rings are made of billions of chunks of water ice, from dust grains to boulders, each one orbiting the planet as an independent moon. The whole system spans roughly 170,000 miles yet averages only about ten yards from top to bottom. Proportionally, it is one of the flattest structures known. The planet inside the rings is stranger than the rings themselves. Saturn is nearly all hydrogen and helium. It has no surface. Its density is lower than water, the only planet in the solar system of which that is true. Its winds reach more than a thousand miles per hour. At its north pole sits a hexagon, a six-sided jet stream almost twenty thousand miles across, holding its corners steady for decades. Nobody built it. It is what happens when a fluid rotating at the right speed meets a faster stream inside it. Then the Cassini spacecraft, which orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, weighed the rings. The result unsettled people. Light, young rings. The best estimates now put them somewhere between ten and a hundred million years old, a blink beside the planet's four and a half billion. Worse, Cassini watched the ice draining steadily into Saturn's atmosphere, a slow fall astronomers call ring rain. On that budget the rings have perhaps a hundred million years left. Saturn has almost certainly spent most of its life bare, and will spend most of the rest bare too. The rings are not a feature of the planet. They are an event. We happen to be alive during it.

6.title: The Planet That Would Float
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Second largest planet, over 700 Earths by volume
Density about 0.69 g/cm3, the only planet less dense than water
Rings roughly 170,000 miles wide, about 10 yards thick
Hexagonal polar jet stream nearly 20,000 miles across
Titan has methane lakes and a thick nitrogen atmosphere
Enceladus vents water and organics from a hidden ocean
Cassini burned up in Saturn on September 15, 2017

blocks.prompt: The Spacecraft That Chose to Burn
blocks.text: On September 15, 2017, a spacecraft the size of a school bus aimed itself at Saturn and gave up its own ability to survive. Cassini had orbited the planet for thirteen years. It was still working. Its cameras were fine, its instruments were fine, and mission control destroyed it on purpose. Understanding why means understanding what Cassini found. Saturn itself is a fair candidate for the strangest object in the solar system. It is the second largest planet, with room inside for more than seven hundred Earths, and it is made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium. It has no surface to land on. Its density is lower than that of water, which makes it the only planet that would bob rather than sink in a sufficiently enormous ocean. Its equatorial winds run past a thousand miles per hour. Over its north pole a jet stream has arranged itself into a hexagon nearly twenty thousand miles wide, six clean sides that have held their shape for at least the forty years humans have been watching. The rings are the famous part, and Cassini rewrote them. Seen from Earth they look like a smooth disk. They are not. They are billions of independent chunks of nearly pure water ice, ranging from grains of dust to boulders, each on its own orbit, packed so tightly that the whole crowd behaves like a fluid. The system spans about 170,000 miles and averages roughly ten yards in thickness. Cassini's final maneuver, twenty-two dives through the narrow gap between the planet and the innermost ring, let it feel the pull of the rings directly and weigh them. They came out light. Low mass implies youth, because ring ice darkens as it gathers dust over time, and this ice is still bright. Current estimates place the rings between ten and a hundred million years old. Saturn is four and a half billion. The rings are also draining away, pulled down into the atmosphere as ring rain fast enough to empty them within another hundred million years. The ornament we treat as permanent is a temporary condition, and we arrived during it. Then there are the moons, and they explain the ending. Titan, the largest, wears a thick nitrogen atmosphere and holds rivers and lakes of liquid methane, the only body besides Earth with stable liquid on its surface. Enceladus, far smaller, sprays plumes of water and simple organic molecules from cracks near its south pole, evidence of a salty ocean under its ice shell. Cassini flew through those plumes and tasted them. That discovery sealed Cassini's fate. The spacecraft was running out of fuel, and an uncontrolled derelict eventually crashes somewhere. If a single Earth microbe had survived the launch and the journey and later landed in the ocean of Enceladus, an unrepeatable experiment would be ruined, and worse, any future discovery of life there could never be trusted. So the engineers chose to burn the spacecraft in Saturn's atmosphere, where nothing could be contaminated. Cassini transmitted data until friction tore it apart. The final signal took eighty-three minutes to cross the distance, arriving from a machine that had already been gone for over an hour.
